title: At 14, Indian American Aryash Shyam Wins a National Writing Prize — and Global Essay Honours
excerpt: A Lehigh Valley ninth-grader's story of a 1776 printer's apprentice won the American Writers Museum prize, capping a year that also brought ANSI and John Locke recognition.
body:
• Aryash Shyam, 14, a ninth-grader in Pennsylvania's Lehigh Valley, has won a national writing prize for historical fiction set in a Philadelphia print shop on July 4, 1776.
  • His story, "The Weight of Lead," is one of four middle-school winners of the American Writers Museum's 2026 John Estey competition and carries a $1,000 prize.
  • In September he also took first place in the high-school category of the ANSI student paper competition — months after finishing middle school.
  • All three of his entries to the John Locke Institute Global Essay Prize were shortlisted from 100,227 entries worldwide, earning two Very High Commendations and one High Commendation.

At 14, Aryash Shyam is collecting writing honours faster than most students collect extracurriculars. The Indian American ninth-grader from Pennsylvania's Lehigh Valley has been named one of four middle-school winners of the 2026 John Estey Student Writing Competition, presented by the American Writers Museum in Chicago, for a piece of historical fiction set on the day the Declaration of Independence was printed, according to Indian American Community News. The award carries a $1,000 prize, and the museum has published the winning work.

A printer's apprentice, and a contradiction

"The Weight of Lead" follows Will, a 13-year-old printer's apprentice setting the type for the Declaration in a Philadelphia print shop on July 4, 1776. As he handles the lead letters, Will becomes aware of another boy whose prospects for freedom are very different from his own — the gap between the document's promise that all men are created equal and the reality of who that promise covered. Aryash has said he grew up paying attention to how everyday things work, reading widely on his own; the story turns that habit on the mechanics of printing itself, and on what the words being printed actually meant.

"I always found myself paying attention to how everyday things work."

— Aryash Shyam, via Indian American Community News

Writing honours beyond his grade

The Estey prize is the latest in a run. In September, Aryash won first place in the high-school category of the 2026 American National Standards Institute Student Paper Competition — as a student who had finished middle school only months earlier — for a paper on how the ISO 80369 standards family redesigned medical tubing connectors so incompatible systems cannot be connected by mistake. The paper drew on his own experience as a surgical patient at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia. Separately, all three of his submissions to the 2026 John Locke Institute Global Essay Prize, in economics, philosophy and science and technology, were shortlisted from 100,227 entries worldwide; the economics and philosophy essays received Very High Commendations and the science and technology essay a High Commendation, according to his own site, which also notes his invitation to the institute's London awards events in October.

The science side

Writing is only one lane. Aryash was one of five recipients of the 2026 Genes in Space Junior Scientist Award, chosen from 130 submissions, for a proposal to validate a cell-free CRISPR diagnostic in microgravity. He built GreenBeam, an AI-powered robot that uses computer vision and a precision laser to target weeds without chemical herbicides, which earned Pennsylvania State Merit recognition in the 2025 3M Young Scientist Challenge. He also hosts Teen Scientist, a monthly programme on WDIY 88.1 FM, the Lehigh Valley's NPR member station, interviewing researchers on subjects from AI to space biology, and made a documentary on the ethics of gene editing.

Why it resonates

For diaspora families, the through-line is the one his teachers keep naming: the same curiosity moves from a 1776 print shop to a standards paper drawn from a hospital stay to a CRISPR proposal for orbit. The next test is public — the John Locke awards events in London this month, where a Lehigh Valley ninth-grader's essays will be read alongside the best of a six-figure global field. Families interested in the competition itself can read the winning story via the American Bazaar's coverage.
